title: Finite type algebras preserve Noetherian spectra
statement: Let $R$ and $B$ be commutative rings with identity and let $R\to B$ be a unital homomorphism. Suppose that $B$ is generated as an $R$-algebra by finitely many elements, equivalently there is a surjective $R$-algebra map $R[x_1,\ldots,x_d]\to B$ for some integer $d\geq0$. If the Zariski topological space underlying $\operatorname{Spec}R$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] is Noetherian, then the Zariski topological space underlying $\operatorname{Spec}B$ is Noetherian. Here a topological space is Noetherian if every ascending chain of open subsets stabilizes; no ascending-chain condition on all ideals of $R$ is assumed. Zero rings are permitted.

source.place: J. Ohm and R. L. Pendleton, Rings with Noetherian spectrum, Duke Math. J. 35 (1968), pp. 631–639, Theorem 2.5 (polynomial extension) and Corollary 2.6 (finite type algebras). WANTED: not present in the local literature collection.

proof.text: We use the descending-closed-chain form of Noetherianity, equivalent to the stated ascending-open-chain form by complements. Three elementary consequences will be used explicitly. A closed subspace of a Noetherian space is Noetherian, since its closed subsets are closed in the ambient space. A space which is the union of two Noetherian subspaces is Noetherian: restrict a descending chain of closed subsets to the two subspaces, take the maximum of their stabilization indices, and take their union. Finally, induction on closed subsets of a Noetherian space is valid: a nonempty collection of counterexamples without a minimal member would, by recursively choosing a strictly smaller member, give a strictly descending chain of closed subsets, contrary to the hypothesis.

source.place: Noetherian spaces, definition-noetherian and lemma-Noetherian (Tag 0052); the chain and induction arguments are written here.

proof.text: First prove the one-variable assertion for an arbitrary ring $R$ with Noetherian spectrum. Put $X=\operatorname{Spec}R$, $Y=\operatorname{Spec}R[T]$, and let $\pi:Y\to X$ be contraction along the constant-polynomial map. This is continuous because $\pi^{-1}(V(J))=V(JR[T])$ for every ideal $J\subseteq R$, directly by membership of constants in a prime. For each closed subset $Z\subseteq X$, the inductive claim $P(Z)$ is that $\pi^{-1}(Z)$, with its subspace topology, is Noetherian. Assume $P(Z')$ for every proper closed subset $Z'\subsetneq Z$. If $Z=\varnothing$ the claim holds. If $Z$ is nonempty and reducible, write $Z=Z_1\cup Z_2$ with both $Z_i$ proper closed subsets of $Z$, hence of $X$. The induction hypothesis applies to both inverse images, and the union argument in step 1 proves $P(Z)$. It remains to prove $P(Z)$ for nonempty irreducible $Z$.

source.place: Paragraph (2), affine-chart Noetherianity input; agent proof, induction claim and its empty/reducible cases.

proof.text: Write the remaining nonempty irreducible closed subset as $Z=V(J)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-spec-quotient-homeomorphism-zero-locus], $\operatorname{Spec}(R/J)$ is homeomorphic to $Z$. It is irreducible, so its entire space is an irreducible component. By [lem-weil-pbc-spec-irreducible-components-minimal-primes], that component is $V(\mathfrak q)$ for a minimal prime $\mathfrak q\subset R/J$. Pull $\mathfrak q$ back to the prime $\mathfrak p\subset R$; the quotient prime correspondence in the first cited statement gives $Z=V(\mathfrak p)$. Put $C=R/\mathfrak p$, an integral domain: the quotient is nonzero and a product of two nonzero classes cannot be zero by primality of $\mathfrak p$. The coefficientwise surjection $R[T]\to C[T]$ has kernel $\mathfrak pR[T]$: a polynomial lies in that kernel exactly when all its finitely many coefficients lie in $\mathfrak p$, and such a polynomial is the sum of those coefficients times powers of $T$. Apply the same quotient-spectrum statement to this surjection. It identifies $\pi^{-1}(Z)=V(\mathfrak pR[T])$ homeomorphically with $\operatorname{Spec}C[T]$. In these identifications the contraction maps to $Z=\operatorname{Spec}C$ agree, since they take the same constant coefficients to the same prime ideals.

source.place: Tags 00E5 (lemma-spec-closed) and 00ES (lemma-irreducible, part (3)); polynomial quotient identification written coefficientwise.

proof.text:
Here is the algebraic argument needed over this domain $C$; it requires no Noetherian-ring hypothesis. Let $I\subseteq C[T]$ be any nonzero ideal. Choose a nonzero $f\in I$ of least degree $n$, and let $a\ne0$ be its leading coefficient. In the localization $C_a$ of [def-weil-ring-localization-away], put $h=a^{-1}f$, which is monic of degree $n$. By [lem-weil-pbc-monic-quotient-free], the classes of $1,T,\ldots,T^{n-1}$ form a $C_a$-basis of $C_a[T]/(h)$. Thus any $g\in I$ has an expression $g=qh+r$ in $C_a[T]$, with $r=0$ or $\deg r<n$: represent the class of $g$ in that basis, and the difference is in the kernel $(h)$ of the quotient map. Multiply $g-qa^{-1}f=r$ by a sufficiently large $a^N$ so that every coefficient of $a^Nr$ and $a^{N-1}q$ belongs to $C$: choose $N\ge1$ larger than the finitely many denominator exponents. Then
$$a^Nr=a^Ng-(a^{N-1}q)f\in I\subseteq C[T].$$
Localization is injective because $C$ is a domain and $a\ne0$, by the fraction equality in the localization definition. Therefore a nonzero $r$ would give a nonzero polynomial $a^Nr\in I$ of degree less than $n$, contrary to minimality. Hence $r=0$. Every image of $g\in I$ is divisible by $h$, and $h=a^{-1}f$ itself belongs to the extended ideal, so $IC_a[T]=(h)$. If $n=0$ the quotient basis is empty and $r$ is already zero. The argument is carried by this step and is not a new node.

source.place: Tag 00CO (definition-localization); Tag 04GG (lemma-characterize-henselian), finite free monic-quotient fact used by the cited node. Agent minimal-degree argument, written out.

proof.text: Take an arbitrary descending chain $F_1\supseteq F_2\supseteq\cdots$ of closed subsets of $\operatorname{Spec}C[T]$. For each $i$ let $I_i$ be the intersection of all prime ideals belonging to $F_i$, taking the whole ring if $F_i=\varnothing$. Then $I_i$ is an ideal, $I_i\subseteq I_{i+1}$, and $V(I_i)=F_i$. Indeed, write $F_i=V(K_i)$; every prime in $F_i$ contains $I_i$ by definition, while $K_i\subseteq I_i$ implies $V(I_i)\subseteq V(K_i)$. The increasing union $I=\bigcup_i I_i$ is an ideal. If $I=0$, every $I_i=0$ and the chain is constant. Otherwise take $f,a,h$ from step 4, and choose $i_0$ with $f\in I_{i_0}$. For every $i\ge i_0$, the extended ideal $I_iC_a[T]$ contains $h$ and is contained in $IC_a[T]=(h)$, so it equals $(h)$. Coefficientwise localization identifies $(C[T])_a$ with $C_a[T]$: a polynomial with fraction coefficients has a common denominator $a^N$, and equality follows coefficientwise from the fraction relation proved for this localization in step 4. By [lem-weil-pbc-spec-localization-away-basic-open](ii), $\operatorname{Spec}C_a[T]$ is the open $D(a)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}C[T]$. A localized prime contains $I_iC_a[T]$ exactly when its contracted prime contains $I_i$. Consequently all the restrictions $F_i\cap D(a)$ agree for $i\ge i_0$.

source.place: Tag 00E4 (lemma-standard-open); agent increasing-ideal and least-degree stabilization argument.

proof.text: The complementary closed subset $V(a)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}C$ is proper because the zero prime of the domain $C$ does not contain $a\ne0$. Under $\operatorname{Spec}C=Z$ its image is a proper closed subset $Z'\subsetneq Z$, hence closed in $X$. The induction hypothesis $P(Z')$ says that $\pi^{-1}(Z')$ is Noetherian. Under step 3's identification this is exactly $V(a)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}C[T]$: both consist of primes whose contraction contains $a$. Thus the restricted chain $F_i\cap V(a)$ stabilizes, say for $i\ge i_1$. Step 5 and the cover $\operatorname{Spec}C[T]=D(a)\cup V(a)$ now give $F_i=F_{\max(i_0,i_1)}$ for all larger $i$. The case $I=0$ was already constant. Every descending closed chain therefore stabilizes, establishing $P(Z)$ in the irreducible case. The induction of step 2 gives $P(X)$, that is, $\operatorname{Spec}R[T]$ is Noetherian. Only topological Noetherianity of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ was assumed.

source.place: Paragraph (2), affine-chart Noetherianity input; agent proof, closed complement and completion of the explicitly stated induction.

proof.text: Apply the one-variable result repeatedly, starting with $R$ and adjoining $x_1,\ldots,x_d$. Ordinary induction on $d$ shows that $\operatorname{Spec}R[x_1,\ldots,x_d]$ is Noetherian; the zero-variable case is the given $\operatorname{Spec}R$. By finite generation in the hypothesis, there is a surjection $R[x_1,\ldots,x_d]\to B$. By [lem-weil-pbc-spec-quotient-homeomorphism-zero-locus], $\operatorname{Spec}B$ is homeomorphic to the closed subset defined by its kernel. It is Noetherian by the closed-subspace chain argument of step 1. If $B=0$ the closed subspace is empty. If $R=0$, a unital $R$-algebra is also zero. Thus all the permitted zero-ring cases are included, proving exactly the stated conclusion.

source.place: Tag 00E5 (lemma-spec-closed); agent finite-variable induction and finite-type quotient step.
